<meta>continues from previous page: the word "asaṃsraṣṭaḥ" (unmixed) split across the break was translated on the previous page; the sentence describing the higher Self continues here</meta>

the Supreme <note>original: "paraḥ"; the OCR's following word "anakān" is unclear and probably corrupt</note> is the Great Lord, all-knowing, the maker <note>original: "sakala-jagan-mātṛ", literally "the measurer" or "mother" of the whole world</note> and ordainer of the whole world. How is he to be known? By inference, or by <unclear>śramāt</unclear> <note>the reading "śramāt", "by toil", looks corrupt; "āgamāt", "by scripture", would be expected alongside inference</note>. For it is like this. The inference runs: "The perceived world under dispute has a cause, because it comes to be after not having been <note>the OCR reads "babhūtvā"; the sense requires "abhūtvā bhāvitvāt", "because of coming into being after not being"</note>, like a painting." After that, what has been understood in general through inference is known in its particulars through yoga. The other, the individual soul <note><term>jīva</term> <gloss>the embodied self</gloss></note>, is established simply by one's own experience. Nature <note><term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>primal matter, the unconscious source of the world</gloss></note> becomes active so that the difference between these two, the higher and the lower, may be known. Its acting for the sake of another will be explained later. And as to its acting for its own sake: towards whichever conscious being <note><term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>the spirit or witness</gloss></note> it has displayed itself through discrimination, towards him it ceases to act <note>original: "udāste", literally "sits apart, becomes indifferent"</note>. How can unconscious nature become active? Activity is observed even in unconscious things, such as milk, for the sake of a result such as the nourishment of a calf <note>the classic Sāṃkhya example: milk flows of itself to feed the calf</note>. ॥ 1 ॥

Next, to the question "Who are qualified for liberation?", he says:

Sūtra: Of the one who is free from passion, because for him it is accomplished. ॥ 2 ॥ <note>original: "viraktasya tatsiddheḥ"</note>

And so scripture says: "Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth and the desire for worlds, they then go about living as mendicants," and: "Having become calm, controlled, withdrawn, patient and collected, he sees the Self within the Self alone." <note>Both quotations come from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.</note> ॥ 2 ॥

If liberation follows upon hearing the teaching, because of dispassion, then everyone would be liberated after receiving a teacher's instruction; and that is not what we see. To this he says:

Sūtra: It is not accomplished by hearing alone, because of the strength of beginningless latent impressions. ॥ 3 ॥ <note>original: "na śravaṇamātrāt tatsiddhir anādivāsanāyā balavattvāt"; <term>vāsanā</term> <gloss>the residual impressions left by past actions and experiences</gloss></note>

Liberation does not follow straight after hearing; rather, because of the strength of the beginningless latent impressions, liberation is swift in one case and comes only after a long time in another. <note>The commentary is very compressed here: the force of the latent impressions decides whether liberation comes quickly or slowly.</note> ॥ 3 ॥

He gives a further reason:

Sūtra: Or, as with one who has many servants, for each one separately. ॥ 4 ॥ <note>The OCR reads "bahubhṛtvavahā pratyekam", which appears to be a corruption of "bahubhṛtyavad vā pratyekam"; it is translated in that sense. The point of the image is explained on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page of a Sāṃkhya commentary describes the Supreme Lord, known by inference and by yoga, and the individual soul, known by experience, and says that nature acts so that the two may be told apart. It then comments on three sūtras: liberation belongs to the dispassionate, it does not come from hearing the teaching alone because of the strength of beginningless latent impressions, and a further reason is introduced through the image of a master with many servants.</summary>
